1.tip: UDP has no handshake, no ISN, no window. The only setup step is picking a random source port.
1.why: UDP is connectionless, so there is no 3-way handshake or window size. The client just picks a random source port so the reply can find its way back to the right app.

2.tip: Guarantee = TCP. Session setup = handshake. UDP has no ACK flag or sequence numbers.
2.why: TCP sets up every session with the 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), so both sides confirm they are ready before data flows. UDP has no handshake at all.

3.why: Well-known ports run from 0 to 1023 and are used by common services like HTTP (80) and DNS (53). 1024 to 49151 are registered ports.

4.tip: Socket = IP + port. Like a street address (IP) plus an apartment number (port).
4.why: A socket pairs an IP address with a port number, such as 192.168.1.5:80. The source socket and destination socket together identify one conversation.

5.why: The window is how many bytes can be sent before an ACK is needed. 1000 bytes split into 100-byte segments is 10 segments.

6.tip: The RECEIVER sets the window: it says how much it can handle at one time.
6.why: The window size is set by the receiving device, based on how much data it can buffer and process at once. This is how TCP flow control stops the sender from overwhelming it.

7.cue: client has UDP datagrams to send
7.tip: UDP = Just Send It. No SYN, no handshake, no asking first.
7.why: UDP is connectionless. It does not check if the server is ready and does not use SYN flags. It simply sends the datagrams.

8.cue: fields in a UDP segment header
8.tip: UDP header has only 4 fields: Source Port, Destination Port, Length, Checksum. No window, no sequence, no ACK.
8.why: The UDP header is just 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length and checksum. Window size, sequence and acknowledgment numbers belong only to TCP.

9.cue: two roles of the transport layer
9.tip: Transport = Track and Identify (ports). Frames and CRC are data link jobs.
9.why: The transport layer uses port numbers to pick the right application and tracks each separate conversation. Framing and CRC checks happen at the data link layer.

10.tip: Sequence numbers put the segments back in SEQUENCE, like page numbers in a book.
10.why: Each TCP segment carries a sequence number, so the receiver can put segments back in the right order even if they arrive mixed up.

11.cue: added to the TCP/IP transport layer header
11.tip: Transport header = ports. Network header = IP addresses. Data link = MAC addresses.
11.why: The transport layer adds source and destination port numbers so data reaches the right application. Logical (IP) addresses are added at the network layer, physical (MAC) at the data link layer.

12.tip: UDP: fast and no receipts. Tracking and retransmitting are TCP jobs.
12.why: UDP has little overhead, so data arrives with minimal delay. It sends no acknowledgments, so nothing is tracked or resent if lost.

13.tip: You get a FIN, you say ACK: "got it, goodbye".
13.why: When one side sends FIN to end its half of the session, the other side replies with an ACK to confirm it got the FIN. Then it sends its own FIN.

14.tip: DNS uses both: quick UDP lookups for clients, TCP for big zone transfers between servers.
14.why: DNS clients send short queries over UDP port 53 for speed. DNS servers use TCP for zone transfers, which move large amounts of data that must arrive complete.

15.cue: What is a characteristic of UDP?
15.tip: UDP keeps arrival order, not the original order. No sequence numbers to fix it.
15.why: UDP has no sequence numbers, so it passes datagrams up in whatever order they arrive. Datagrams may take different paths, and apps can add their own reliability.

16.tip: You REGISTER with IANA to get a REGISTERED port (1024-49151).
16.why: Registered ports (1024 to 49151) are given out by IANA to companies for specific applications. Dynamic or private ports are picked freely by clients.

17.tip: TCP: email, files, web (SMTP, FTP, HTTP). UDP: the simple ones (SNMP, TFTP, DHCP).
17.why: Email, file transfers and web pages must arrive complete, so SMTP, FTP and HTTP use TCP. SNMP, TFTP and DHCP use UDP for speed and low overhead.

keys.k: application layer protocols for error detection

18.tip: UDP = connectionless, low overhead, lets the app handle errors. It is Layer 4, not Layer 3.
18.why: UDP is a simple, connectionless Layer 4 protocol with no sequencing or flow control. If an application needs error recovery, the application has to do it itself.

19.cue: in the TCP header but not in the UDP header
19.tip: Both have ports and checksum. Only TCP has window and sequence (for flow control and ordering).
19.why: Both headers have source port, destination port and checksum. TCP adds sequence numbers for ordering and a window field for flow control, which UDP does not do.

20.tip: Control bits = the flags (SYN, ACK, FIN). Flags show the handshake state.
20.why: The control bits field holds flags like SYN, ACK and FIN. These flags show which step of the handshake or teardown a segment is part of.

21.tip: A web page with missing pieces is broken. HTTP needs reliable = TCP.
21.why: A web page must arrive complete and in order, so HTTP needs TCP's reliable delivery with acknowledgments and resending. Speed and best-effort describe UDP.

22.tip: UDP fits apps that fix errors on their own, or that want speed over perfection (voice, video).
22.why: UDP gives no reliability, so it suits apps that handle it themselves or that can lose a little data but need low delay, like live voice. Flow control and reordering are TCP jobs.

keys.k: source port number is used to track

23.tip: Same service, many chats: the destination port is the same, so the SOURCE port tells them apart.
23.why: When you open several sessions to the same service, they all share one destination port. Each gets its own random source port, which keeps the conversations separate.

24.tip: UDP = fast and no promises. TCP = slower but guaranteed.
24.why: UDP skips the acknowledgments and ordering that TCP does, so it's faster with less overhead. Use it when speed matters more than every packet arriving, like voice or video.

25.cue: three responsibilities of the transport layer
25.tip: Transport: Reliability, Multiplexing, Identifying apps. Routing is network, formatting is presentation, frames are data link.
25.why: The transport layer meets reliability needs, mixes many conversations onto one network, and uses ports to find the right app. Routing packets is the network layer's job.

26.tip: Discover = a new client shouting to everyone (broadcast 255.255.255.255). Only the server answers.
26.why: A client with no address sends Discover as a broadcast to 255.255.255.255, so every host gets it, but only a DHCP server replies. Its source MAC is the client's own MAC, not all ones.

27.tip: Sending mail: DNS finds the mail server, SMTP sends it. POP and IMAP are for receiving.
27.why: To send email, the device uses DNS to find the mail server's address and SMTP to deliver the message. POP3 and IMAP are only used to retrieve mail.

28.tip: SMB stays connected: one long session to the file server. Compare FTP, which opens a new data link per transfer.
28.why: SMB clients set up a long-term connection to the server and use it to reach shared files and printers. SMB messages share one format and can authenticate sessions.

29.cue: function of the HTTP GET message
29.tip: GET = get a page. POST and PUT = send or upload to the server.
29.why: A web browser sends an HTTP GET to ask a web server for a page. Uploading uses POST or PUT, and getting email on port 110 is POP3.

30.cue: interface between the applications and the underlying network
30.tip: The application layer is the top layer, closest to you: it's where your apps meet the network.
30.why: The application layer is the top OSI layer. It gives programs like browsers and email clients a way to use the network to send their messages.

31.cue: uploads one chapter document to a file server
31.tip: File SERVER in the question = client/server model.
31.why: The author's computer is the client, and the publisher's file server stores and serves files. A dedicated server receiving requests is the client/server model.

32.tip: Both models have clients and servers. The difference: P2P has no DEDICATED server.
32.why: In both models some device acts as a server and some as a client. In peer-to-peer a single device can play both roles, and there is no dedicated server.

33.tip: BitTorrent and friends share straight between users: peer-to-peer.
33.why: These apps share files or data directly between users' computers with no central server, which is the peer-to-peer model.

34.tip: The "Share" apps speak Gnutella. Link: Gnu-tella tells peers what you have.
34.why: Gnutella is a peer-to-peer protocol that lets users find and share files on each other's computers. Apps like Bearshare and Shareaza use it.

35.tip: Peer-to-peer = equals sharing, no boss server.
35.why: In a peer-to-peer network, each device shares its own resources directly with others. No dedicated server is needed. A print server would be client/server.

36.cue: TCP/IP application layer performs functions of OSI
36.tip: Top 3 OSI layers (5, 6, 7) squeeze into TCP/IP's one application layer.
36.why: The TCP/IP model has one application layer that covers the top three OSI layers: session, presentation and application.

37.tip: DNS has a server answering requests = client/server. eMule and a coworker's shared printer are P2P.
37.why: The workstation is a DNS client asking a DNS server to turn www.cisco.com into an IP address. eMule and sharing a coworker's printer are peer-to-peer, and ARP is not a client/server app.

38.tip: Trap: "presentation" is OSI. In TCP/IP the application layer does it all.
38.why: In OSI, formatting, compression and encryption are presentation layer jobs. TCP/IP has no presentation layer, so its application layer does this work.

39.tip: SMB: one long session. FTP: two connections and a new one per transfer. Both use TCP.
39.why: An SMB client keeps a long-term connection to the server for many file actions. FTP is the one that uses two connections, and both protocols run over TCP.

40.tip: Web = HTTP, File = FTP, Mail = SMTP.
40.why: HTTP serves web pages, FTP transfers files and SMTP sends email. DNS, SNMP and DHCP are support services, not these three apps.

41.tip: GET, PUT, POST are what a browser says to a web server: HTTP.
41.why: HTTP uses GET to ask for a page, POST to send data, and PUT to upload a file. The other protocols use different message types.

42.tip: MX = Mail eXchange. A = address, NS = name server, CNAME = alias.
42.why: An MX record tells which mail servers accept email for a domain. An A record holds an IP address, NS points to a name server and CNAME is an alias.

43.cue: protocols at the application layer of TCP/IP
43.tip: TCP and UDP are transport. ARP is the odd one out. FTP, POP3, DHCP are the apps.
43.why: FTP, POP3 and DHCP are services that applications use, so they sit at the application layer. TCP and UDP are transport protocols, and ARP works below them.

44.cue: communicate securely with a web server
44.tip: S for Secure: HTTPS = HTTP encrypted.
44.why: HTTPS is HTTP with encryption (TLS), so a web client can talk to a web server safely. SMTP and IMAP are email, and SMB is file sharing.

45.cue: act as client and server at the same time
45.tip: P2P: every peer both asks and serves.
45.why: In peer-to-peer (P2P) applications each device can request files and share files at the same time, so it acts as both client and server.

46.tip: P2P = spread out (decentralized), no dedicated server. It does NOT scale well.
46.why: In P2P networks the resources sit on each user's device, not in one place, and there is no dedicated server. That makes them hard to scale and to manage user accounts.

47.cue: function provided by the transport layer
47.tip: Two browser windows = two source ports. Transport sorts which data goes to which window.
47.why: Each browser window uses its own source port, so the transport layer can send each page back to the right window. A burned-in ID is a MAC address, and screen formatting is the presentation job.

48.cue: OSI similar to the TCP/IP application layer
48.tip: OSI top three (Session, Presentation, Application) = TCP/IP application. Remember "All People Seem".
48.why: The single TCP/IP application layer does the work of OSI layers 5, 6 and 7: session, presentation and application. Transport is its own layer in both models.

49.tip: ACK = bytes received + 1. 2 x 1500 = 3000, so ACK 3001.
49.why: TCP acknowledges with the number of the next byte it expects. After two 1,500-byte packets it has bytes 1 to 3000, so it asks for byte 3001.

50.tip: ACK = bytes received + 1. 3 x 1500 = 4500, so ACK 4501.
50.why: TCP's ACK names the next byte it wants. Three 1,500-byte packets cover bytes 1 to 4500, so the server acknowledges 4501.

51.tip: ACK = bytes received + 1. 4 x 1500 = 6000, so ACK 6001.
51.why: The ACK number is the next byte expected. Four 1,500-byte packets fill the 6,000-byte window, bytes 1 to 6000, so the ACK is 6001.

52.why: TFTP, a simple file transfer protocol, listens on UDP port 69. The client puts 69 as the destination port so the server knows which service is wanted.

53.tip: FTP control = 21 (data uses 20). FTP 21, SSH 22, Telnet 23 count up.
53.why: FTP servers listen for commands on TCP port 21, so the client uses 21 as the destination port. Port 20 carries the actual file data.

54.tip: SSH = 22, right between FTP 21 and Telnet 23.
54.why: SSH, the secure remote login service, uses TCP port 22. The client sends to destination port 22 to reach it.

55.why: Web servers listen for plain HTTP on TCP port 80, so the browser uses 80 as the destination port.

56.tip: POP3 = 110. Think "POP 1-1-0". IMAP is 143, SMTP is 25.
56.why: POP3, used to download email from a mail server, listens on TCP port 110.

57.tip: Telnet = 23, one after SSH 22. SSH is the secure upgrade.
57.why: Telnet, the old unencrypted remote login service, uses TCP port 23.

58.why: SNMP, used to monitor and manage network devices, listens on UDP port 161.

59.tip: SMTP = 25. Send Mail To People on port 25.
59.why: SMTP, which sends email between clients and servers, uses TCP port 25.

60.why: Secure web traffic (HTTPS) uses TCP port 443, so the browser sends to destination port 443.

61.tip: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK: each side says goodbye and the other confirms. No SYN in a teardown.
61.why: The client sends FIN to close its side, the server ACKs it, then the server sends its own FIN, and the client ACKs that. SYN is only for opening a session.
